claims.text: The baseline CoCrFeMnNi alloy is equiatomic.
The as-solidified CoCrFeMnNi baseline has a single-phase FCC microstructure.
The as-solidified Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy has a single-phase FCC microstructure.
The Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy has a higher stacking-fault energy than equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
Higher stacking-fault energy in the Co-free alloy suppresses deformation-twin nucleation.
Higher stacking-fault energy in the Co-free alloy promotes dislocation cross-slip and cross-slip-driven dynamic recovery.
The shift from twinning to cross-slip stabilizes work hardening.
Cross-slip-driven dynamic recovery produces flow without serrations.
The proposed mechanism preserves a favorable strength–ductility balance under dynamic loading from 200 to 700 K and from 10^-3 to 10^3 s^-1.
The controlled comparison consists of uniaxial compression of the two alloys to 0.3 true strain at five temperatures and five strain rates within 200–700 K and 10^-3–10^3 s^-1.
The comparison holds heat treatment and sample geometry constant.
Relative to CoCrFeMnNi, the Co-free alloy will have at least 20% lower twin volume fraction.
Relative to CoCrFeMnNi, the Co-free alloy will have at least 10% higher work-hardening rate.
Relative to CoCrFeMnNi, the Co-free alloy will exhibit reduced flow-stress serrations.
Relative to CoCrFeMnNi, the Co-free alloy will have equal or improved ultimate strength.
Relative to CoCrFeMnNi, the Co-free alloy will have equal or improved ductility.
The hypothesis is restricted to single-phase FCC material, temperatures of 200–700 K, strain rates of 10^-3–10^3 s^-1, and true strains no greater than 0.3.
A paired test at 300 K, 10^2 s^-1, and 0.25 true strain can distinguish the alloys by TEM twin fraction, work-hardening rate, and serration amplitude.

contradictions.description: The mechanism predicts flow without serrations, whereas the outcome predicts only reduced serrations, allowing residual serrations.

The falsification test specifies deformation to 0.25 true strain for post-mortem characterization but also lists total compressive strain to failure; a specimen stopped at 0.25 strain cannot simultaneously provide strain-to-failure unless a separate test is performed.
